# Emerging Technologies Enhancing the Security of Mobile Voting

## 1\. Technological Innovations in Secure Mobile Voting

Modern mobile voting systems are leveraging cutting-edge technologies to bolster security. Key innovations include **blockchain ledgers**, **biometric authentication**, **end-to-end encryption (E2EE)** with verifiability, and **secure multi-party computation (MPC)** techniques. Each of these plays a distinct role in improving voter authentication, protecting data integrity and privacy, and resisting threats:

-   **Blockchain Technology:** Distributed ledger technology introduces decentralization and immutability to ballot records. Instead of a single database, votes are recorded in blocks replicated across multiple nodes, making tampering extremely difficult. Once a vote is recorded and verified by the network of servers (“verifiers”), it cannot be altered without detection[new.voatz.com](https://new.voatz.com/faq/what-is-blockchain-and-how-does-it-work-for-voatz/#:~:text=Blockchain%20is%20sometimes%20referred%20to,entire%20network%20of%20verifying%20servers)[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=Similarly%2C%20mobile%20voting%20offers%20a,by%20the%20county%20elections%20office). This transparency and permanence help **prevent fraud and manipulation**, and increase trust that results reflect the true votes cast[mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/1/17#:~:text=Blockchain%20technology%20has%20been%20recognized,associated%20with%20traditional%20voting%20systems)[mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/1/17#:~:text=traditional%20and%20other%20e,cryptographic%20techniques%20and%20consensus%20protocols). For example, the Voatz mobile voting platform uses a permissioned blockchain (with numerous verifying servers) to log every cast ballot; if an attacker tried to change a vote on one server, the discrepancy would be caught by others maintaining the ledger[new.voatz.com](https://new.voatz.com/faq/what-is-blockchain-and-how-does-it-work-for-voatz/#:~:text=geographically%20separated%20servers,servers%20and%20cannot%20be%20changed)[new.voatz.com](https://new.voatz.com/faq/what-is-blockchain-and-how-does-it-work-for-voatz/#:~:text=Once%20submitted%2C%20the%20votes%20for,additional%20voters%20submit%20their%20selections). Blockchain’s **tamper-evident** design thus strengthens data integrity and provides an auditable trail of all votes. However, blockchains must be carefully implemented to ensure they also preserve voter anonymity and can scale to high volumes (scalability remains an area for improvement[mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/1/17#:~:text=auditability%20receive%20significant%20attention%2C%20they,aspect%20of%20scalability%20needs%20attention)).
-   **Biometric Authentication:** Mobile voting apps increasingly incorporate biometrics (like fingerprint or facial recognition) as part of multi-factor login to **verify the voter’s identity**. This ensures that the person casting a ballot on a device is indeed the authorized voter. For instance, in West Virginia’s 2018 pilot, voters had to scan a government photo ID, take a live selfie for facial comparison, and then were required to use the phone’s fingerprint or FaceID to authenticate each time they accessed the ballot[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=cursory%20identifying%20information%20like%20a,prevent%20fraud%20or%20voter%20impersonation). Tying the voter’s credentials to unique biometrics makes impersonation or multiple voting far more difficult. After initial verification, Voatz links the voter’s account to their fingerprint/face or a PIN stored securely on the smartphone, and all the original ID documents and selfies are expunged for privacy[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=Protecting%20all%20voters%E2%80%99%20personal%20information,authenticate%20the%20voter%20going%20forward). Biometric factors thus add a strong layer of **voter authentication**, preventing unauthorized access even if login credentials are stolen. When combined with device security (secure enclaves on modern phones), biometrics help ensure **only legitimate voters cast ballots**, mitigating risks of fraud or vote-selling. (It is worth noting that biometrics must be implemented carefully to accommodate voters who cannot use them and to protect sensitive data.)
-   **End-to-End Encryption and Verifiability:** End-to-end encryption is now a staple for protecting ballot confidentiality in transit and at rest. With E2EE, a voter’s ballot selections are encrypted on their device and remain encrypted until tallied by election authorities, so **no intermediaries can read or alter the vote**[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/how-it-works#:~:text=%23%20End). Even if network traffic is intercepted, the encryption prevents eavesdropping or tampering. Additionally, modern mobile voting solutions emphasize _end-to-end verifiability_ – mechanisms that allow voters and observers to confirm that votes were cast as intended, transmitted securely, and counted accurately. One approach is giving each voter a **secure receipt or tracking code** after they vote. For example, mobile voting systems provide an encrypted, anonymized receipt that the voter can later use to verify their vote was included in the final tally (without revealing their choices)[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=1,If%20the%20votes%20pass%20all). Microsoft’s open-source ElectionGuard toolkit demonstrates this innovation: _each vote is encrypted and given a tracking ID, and voters get a code to check that their encrypted ballot arrived untampered and was counted_[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=What%20does%20ElectionGuard%20do%3F)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=Election%20monitors%20carry%20out%20spot,end%20verifiability). Crucially, the encryption and verification process is designed so that **no one (not even the voter) can prove to a third party how they voted**, in order to preserve secrecy and prevent coercion[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=ElectionGuard%20uses%20something%20called%20homomorphic,that%20their%20vote%20wasn%E2%80%99t%20changed). In sum, end-to-end encryption ensures **ballot privacy and integrity**, while end-to-end verifiability adds transparency – if any vote were altered or dropped, audits would catch it, thereby greatly enhancing **threat resistance** against hacking.
-   **Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) and Homomorphic Tallying:** To address the risks of a single point of failure, secure multi-party computation techniques distribute the trust among multiple parties or servers. In a typical implementation, no single server holds the keys to decrypt votes; instead, decryption or tallying requires a _quorum_ of independent parties, so that a lone attacker cannot compromise the whole election. For example, an election system might split the decryption key among several authorities (election officials, auditors, etc.) – only when they combine their key shares can votes be decrypted, and no individual official ever sees a complete private key. This guards against insider threats and ensures **votes remain secret unless proper procedures are followed**. A related innovation is **homomorphic encryption**, a form of MPC that allows votes to be aggregated while still encrypted. ElectionGuard uses homomorphic encryption to sum up encrypted votes into an encrypted tally, which can then be decrypted by trustees _without ever decrypting individual ballots_[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=ElectionGuard%20uses%20something%20called%20homomorphic,that%20their%20vote%20wasn%E2%80%99t%20changed). This means the voting system can compute results (e.g. total votes per candidate) **without exposing any single vote**, greatly protecting voter privacy. Furthermore, because multiple parties are involved in the decryption and verification (often with public audit tools), any attempt to corrupt the tally would require conspiring across many independent entities – an unlikely scenario. Secure MPC approaches thereby contribute to **robust threat resistance**: they eliminate any single point of attack and make the election outcome verifiable by observers. In practice, these cryptographic methods (homomorphic tallying, threshold decryption, etc.) are being integrated to ensure even a nation-state hacker cannot silently subvert results without detection[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=But%2C%20as%20Josh%20Benaloh%2C%20Senior,state%20attacker.%E2%80%9D)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=Because%20attacks%20cannot%20always%20be,That%20requires%20stringent%20auditing). As these techniques mature, they promise **high-integrity counts** that are transparently correct, all while upholding ballot secrecy.

The table below summarizes how these emerging technologies contribute to security:

| **Technology** | **Security Contribution in Mobile Voting** |
| --- | --- |
| **Blockchain Ledgers** | _Integrity & Auditability:_ Immutable, distributed record prevents undetected tampering. Multiple nodes verify each vote, creating a tamper-proof log and transparent audit trail[mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/1/17#:~:text=Blockchain%20technology%20has%20been%20recognized,associated%20with%20traditional%20voting%20systems)[mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/1/17#:~:text=traditional%20and%20other%20e,cryptographic%20techniques%20and%20consensus%20protocols). Enhances trust that votes aren’t altered and provides forensic evidence against fraud. |
| **Biometric Auth** | _Voter Authentication:_ Fingerprint, facial recognition or similar biometrics confirm the voter’s identity before casting a ballot. Blocks impostors and ensures only legitimate, registered voters access the mobile ballot[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=cursory%20identifying%20information%20like%20a,prevent%20fraud%20or%20voter%20impersonation). Harder to steal or spoof than passwords, thus reducing fraudulent votes and double voting. |
| **End-to-End Encryption** | _Privacy & Data Security:_ Encrypts ballot data from the moment of casting until final counting, so no intermediary can read or modify votes in transit[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/how-it-works#:~:text=%23%20End). Preserves ballot secrecy and guarantees integrity – if anyone tries to alter an encrypted vote, decryption or verification checks will fail. Often paired with receipts or tracking codes that let voters verify inclusion in the tally without revealing their vote[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=Election%20monitors%20carry%20out%20spot,end%20verifiability). |
| **Secure MPC** | _Distributed Trust & Secret Tallying:_ Splits the election computation or decryption across multiple independent parties, ensuring no single server can compromise the election. Homomorphic encryption (an MPC technique) allows direct tallying of encrypted votes, protecting individual ballot secrecy even during count[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=ElectionGuard%20uses%20something%20called%20homomorphic,that%20their%20vote%20wasn%E2%80%99t%20changed). Detects or prevents insider manipulation and mitigates the impact of any one system being hacked. |

## 2\. Implementation Challenges and Security Threats

Implementing mobile voting on a large scale comes with significant technical and operational challenges. Elections are high-stakes events with strict requirements for security, scalability, accessibility, and legal compliance. Below we examine key challenges and how officials and vendors are addressing them:

-   **Scalability and Reliability:** Mobile voting systems must scale to potentially millions of users casting votes in a short time window. This puts heavy demand on server infrastructure and networks. Ensuring the system stays available (and performant) on Election Day is paramount – any outage or slow-down could disenfranchise voters or call results into question. Blockchain-based voting, for instance, raises questions about throughput and latency if every transaction (vote) must be confirmed across a distributed ledger. Research surveys note that while security has been a primary focus of new e-voting designs, the crucial aspect of _scalability_ often needs more attention[mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/1/17#:~:text=aforementioned%20key%20benefits%20in%20the,aspect%20of%20scalability%20needs%20attention). Systems like Voatz’s private blockchain have so far handled the relatively small pilot elections, but the challenge remains to prove such architectures can reliably support **national-level turnout**. Cloud-based deployment and load balancing are used to handle spikes, and rigorous stress-testing is conducted before elections. Another reliability aspect is ensuring votes are **successfully recorded even on poor internet connections** (common for military overseas voters). Solutions include allowing offline vote capture (storing an encrypted vote on the device until connectivity resumes) or fallbacks like reverting to email/fax if the app fails. Election officials must have contingency plans (extended voting windows, help desks, paper alternatives) to mitigate any technical glitches. In short, scaling mobile voting requires robust infrastructure and redundancy akin to online banking systems, but with the added complexity of a fixed deadline and public scrutiny.
-   **Accessibility and Usability:** Voting is a fundamental right, so any mobile solution must be accessible to _all_ eligible voters, including those with disabilities, low digital literacy, or lack of high-end devices. This poses a design challenge: the app must be extremely user-friendly and compliant with accessibility standards (like WCAG for visually impaired users). On one hand, mobile voting can dramatically improve accessibility – for example, voters with physical disabilities who cannot travel or handle paper ballots can vote independently on their personal devices (West Virginia and Utah pilots explicitly extended mobile voting to citizens with disabilities, enabling 217 disabled voters to cast ballots from home in 2020)[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=person%20and%20independently%20by%20mail,any%20internal%20or%20external%20tampering). On the other hand, not every voter owns a smartphone or reliable internet. There is a risk of **digital divide**: rural or elderly voters might be excluded if mobile voting became the primary method. Thus, mobile voting is usually offered as an _optional_ alternative (in pilots it’s often for overseas or disabled voters only, with traditional methods remaining available for others). Usability testing with diverse groups is critical to ensure the interface is intuitive (clear navigation, large text options, etc.) and that voters can verify and submit their ballot without confusion. **Multi-language support** is another requirement in many jurisdictions. To accommodate those without modern devices, some jurisdictions might provide tablet kiosks or assistive devices as needed. In summary, while mobile voting can **improve accessibility** for many (by offering convenience and independence), it must be carefully designed and supplemented with alternatives to avoid disenfranchising anyone.
-   **Cybersecurity Threats:** Mobile voting faces an array of cyber threats familiar to any internet-based system, but with even higher stakes. These threats include:
    **Hacking and Malware –** Attackers may attempt to exploit vulnerabilities in the voting app, servers, or the voter’s device to alter votes or cause disruptions. Independent experts have raised concerns that poorly secured mobile voting apps could allow hackers to change votes undetected[govtech.com](https://www.govtech.com/biz/Detailed-Audit-of-Voatz-Voting-App-Confirms-Security-Flaws.html#:~:text=%E2%80%9COur%20assessment%20confirmed%20the%20issues,security%2C%E2%80%9D%20the%20blog%20post%20says). In fact, a 2020 audit of the Voatz app (used in U.S. pilots) found dozens of security issues and confirmed that an attacker with malware on a voter’s phone might intercept and modify a ballot before it’s encrypted[govtech.com](https://www.govtech.com/biz/Detailed-Audit-of-Voatz-Voting-App-Confirms-Security-Flaws.html#:~:text=assessment%20of%20the%20platform%20to,low%2C%20undetermined%20and%20informational%20severity)[govtech.com](https://www.govtech.com/biz/Detailed-Audit-of-Voatz-Voting-App-Confirms-Security-Flaws.html#:~:text=%E2%80%9COur%20assessment%20confirmed%20the%20issues,security%2C%E2%80%9D%20the%20blog%20post%20says). Similarly, earlier online voting systems have been compromised in testing – for example, researchers in Australia showed they could bypass encryption in a 2015 Scytl-based iVoting system and alter votes, due to vulnerabilities in the code[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=match%20at%20L174%20In%202015%2C,Another%20group%20of%20researchers). These examples underscore the real risk of undetected vote manipulation if strong safeguards are not in place. Mobile devices themselves can be weak links: if a voter’s phone is infected with spyware or a Trojan, it could potentially capture their votes or credentials. **Mitigation:** Vendors are employing secure coding practices, regular penetration tests, and third-party code audits to harden their apps. Using the phone’s secure enclave to store cryptographic keys and employing anti-tampering measures in the app can help protect against malware. Some approaches even consider _software independence_: for instance, generating a parallel paper ballot that can be cross-checked ensures that even a hacked app cannot change the official count without being caught[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=2,record%20alongside%20all%20other%20votes)[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=nodes%20on%20a%20public,record%20alongside%20all%20other%20votes).

    **Phishing and Social Engineering –** Attackers might also target voters directly through phishing emails or fake websites, trying to trick them into revealing login credentials or installing malicious “voting” apps. Since voters aren’t all cybersecurity experts, a well-crafted phishing campaign could impersonate an official election email and redirect voters to a fraudulent portal. Once the voter enters their info, the attacker could cast a fake vote or invalidate their real one. **Mitigation:** Election officials must conduct robust voter education, telling people exactly how they will be contacted and what the legitimate app or login process looks like. Multi-factor authentication (especially biometrics) protects against simple password theft[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/how-it-works#:~:text=%23%20Multi). Some jurisdictions issue _unique voter-specific codes or IDs_ via mail that must be entered into the app, to ensure the person logging in is the intended voter. Regular warnings about not clicking unknown links and providing a hotline for voters to verify communications can reduce phishing success.

    **Denial-of-Service (DoS) Attacks –** A well-timed DDoS attack on the mobile voting servers or network could block or delay voters from casting ballots. Election adversaries might try to overwhelm the system on Election Day to undermine confidence. **Mitigation:** Providers use cloud scaling, content delivery networks, and DDoS protection services to absorb malicious traffic. Additionally, some systems design an “offline” mode (as mentioned earlier) where a voter’s device can queue the vote if servers are unreachable, submitting it when connectivity restores, so a short outage doesn’t prevent voting. Election rules can also help – e.g. accepting ballots that were in queue if a disruption occurs, or extending deadlines if a known attack impacted access.

    **Insider Threats and Supply Chain –** Security isn’t only about outside hackers. The integrity of mobile voting also relies on trusted insiders (developers, election officials) and the supply chain of software updates. A rogue developer could try to insert backdoors, or an update server could be compromised to distribute a malicious app update right before the election. **Mitigation:** Open-source development and public code audits, as practiced by some mobile voting projects, can shine light on the code base[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/how-it-works#:~:text=). Strict internal controls, background checks for personnel, and cryptographic signing of app updates are standard practices to ensure only verified code is deployed. Some jurisdictions require that the final software build used in an election be escrowed and hashed so that anyone can verify the app on their phone matches the certified version.

-   **Verifiability and Audit:** A fundamental challenge is how to **audit and verify** an election that took place on thousands of personal devices. Traditional paper-based elections allow manual recounts and audits of physical ballots; with mobile voting, the records are digital. To gain equal or greater confidence, election officials must implement rigorous end-to-end verification processes. This includes giving voters the means to confirm their votes and enabling independent auditors to validate the overall results. As noted, systems like Voatz produce multiple records: an encrypted receipt for the voter, a paper ballot printed in the jurisdiction, and a blockchain record – all three are cross-checked in a post-election audit to ensure they match[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=1,If%20the%20votes%20pass%20all)[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=There%20is%20an%20additional%20step,Technology%20page%20of%20our%20website). **Risk-limiting audits** can be adapted for digital ballots by comparing a random sample of electronic records to their paper printouts. In West Virginia and Utah’s pilots, third-party observers (e.g. the National Cybersecurity Center) were invited to audit the results, and they reported _no evidence of tampering_ in those trials[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=person%20and%20independently%20by%20mail,any%20internal%20or%20external%20tampering). This kind of transparency is vital to bolstering public confidence. A remaining challenge is convincing skeptics: critics argue that without a voter-verified paper record for every vote, a determined hack might go unnoticed. Thus many experts advocate that **mobile voting should always generate a parallel paper trail** or employ advanced end-to-end verification where voters can independently confirm their vote in the final tally (as ElectionGuard does). Achieving a universally trusted verification method remains an ongoing task for mobile voting technologists.
-   **Compliance and Legal Challenges:** Deploying mobile voting must navigate a complex legal landscape. Election laws in many jurisdictions were written with paper ballots in mind, and adapting them to allow internet or mobile voting can require legislative change. Compliance issues include **meeting statutory requirements** for ballot secrecy, ballot storage, and recounts. For example, some U.S. states mandate a voter-verified paper audit trail for every vote – a requirement that effectively bans pure electronic voting unless a printable record is created. Mobile voting providers have addressed this by producing paper ballots (as Voatz does) or by ensuring an auditable log that officials accept as equivalent. Another challenge is certification: in the U.S., any system used for voting in federal elections usually needs to be tested and certified to federal or state standards. Currently, **no federal certification exists specifically for internet/mobile voting systems**, which creates uncertainty. Each pilot often proceeds under special exemptions or as a form of electronic absentee ballot return authorized for certain voters. This patchwork approach means deployment can be slow and limited. Furthermore, election officials must ensure **chain-of-custody and voter identity rules** are upheld – for instance, verifying that a mobile voter is eligible and hasn’t already voted in-person. Compliance also extends to data protection regulations (protecting voters’ personal data and ensuring systems meet privacy laws like GDPR in Europe). Overall, the legal-operational challenge is aligning these new technologies with existing election frameworks or pushing those frameworks to evolve. Some regions (e.g. Utah as of 2020) have passed laws to enable broader mobile voting pilots, whereas others explicitly prohibit transmitting voted ballots electronically due to security concerns. Navigating this environment requires collaboration between technologists, election administrators, and lawmakers to update regulations in a way that balances innovation with caution.

## 3\. Leading Companies and Solutions in Mobile Voting

Several organizations have taken the lead in developing secure mobile and online voting platforms. Here we profile three prominent players – **Voatz**, **Scytl**, and **ElectionGuard** – examining their technology, deployments, and market impact. Each represents a different approach to the mobile voting challenge, from startup-driven innovation to established election industry expertise and open-source collaboration:

### 3.1 Voatz

Voatz is a U.S.-based startup that has pioneered mobile voting with blockchain technology. Its platform is a mobile app that combines **biometric voter authentication, encrypted cloud storage of ballots, and a permissioned blockchain ledger** to record votes. Voatz emerged around 2016 and gained prominence by conducting the **first smartphone voting pilot in U.S. federal elections**. Notably, West Virginia used Voatz in the 2018 mid-term election for overseas military voters – the first time UOCAVA (military/expat) voters could cast actual ballots via smartphone in a federal election. In that pilot, voters from 24 counties used the Voatz app to verify their identity and submit their ballots, which were then recorded on an immutable blockchain and also printed out at the county election office[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=After%20a%20successful%20test%20run,eligible%20military%20and%20overseas%20civilians)[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=2,record%20alongside%20all%20other%20votes). A post-election audit (with voters able to compare their digital receipt to the printed ballot) found no discrepancies, and officials reported that mobile voting slightly increased turnout among eligible overseas voters (an academic study estimated a **3–5% turnout increase** in West Virginia’s pilot)[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=A%20study%20from%20the%20University,5%20percentage%20points).

**Technology:** Voatz’s system emphasizes a multi-layered security approach. Voter identity proofing is done by scanning a government ID and matching it to a selfie video; once verified, the app relies on the phone’s fingerprint or FaceID for login thereafter[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=Protecting%20all%20voters%E2%80%99%20personal%20information,authenticate%20the%20voter%20going%20forward). Votes are **end-to-end encrypted** on the device and **sent through a secure tunnel** to Voatz’s servers. There, they are anonymized and added as transactions on a blockchain using Hyperledger technology. Multiple independent server nodes validate each ballot transaction, and the distributed ledger ensures that **records cannot be altered or deleted unnoticed**[new.voatz.com](https://new.voatz.com/faq/what-is-blockchain-and-how-does-it-work-for-voatz/#:~:text=Blockchain%20is%20sometimes%20referred%20to,entire%20network%20of%20verifying%20servers)[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=Similarly%2C%20mobile%20voting%20offers%20a,by%20the%20county%20elections%20office). For transparency, Voatz provides each voter with an encrypted receipt and conducts a public “citizens’ audit” after the election, comparing the blockchain records, digital receipts, and paper ballots to prove consistency[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=1,If%20the%20votes%20pass%20all)[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=There%20is%20an%20additional%20step,Technology%20page%20of%20our%20website). In terms of privacy, the use of anonymous voter IDs and encryption is meant to keep votes secret while still enabling verification. Voatz also implements standard cybersecurity practices (bug bounty programs, third-party audits, etc.). An example of their audits: Voatz engaged cybersecurity firm Trail of Bits in 2019 to do a deep review of its platform. The audit (completed in early 2020) did flag some high-severity issues, aligning with an earlier MIT study that pointed out potential vulnerabilities where malware could change a vote before it reached the blockchain[govtech.com](https://www.govtech.com/biz/Detailed-Audit-of-Voatz-Voting-App-Confirms-Security-Flaws.html#:~:text=assessment%20of%20the%20platform%20to,low%2C%20undetermined%20and%20informational%20severity)[govtech.com](https://www.govtech.com/biz/Detailed-Audit-of-Voatz-Voting-App-Confirms-Security-Flaws.html#:~:text=%E2%80%9COur%20assessment%20confirmed%20the%20issues,security%2C%E2%80%9D%20the%20blog%20post%20says). Voatz responded by patching many issues and has maintained that no successful attack has occurred in a live election. The need for continued scrutiny is acknowledged, and Voatz’s openness to audits is a positive sign (though critics wanted more transparency into the blockchain’s contents during live elections).

**Market Footprint & Deployments:** Voatz remains one of the few mobile voting apps that has seen real-world usage in public elections. Beyond West Virginia 2018, it was used in subsequent pilots: _Denver, Colorado_ ran a mobile voting option for overseas voters in its 2019 municipal election (also using Voatz), and _Utah County, Utah_ offered Voatz in 2019 and 2020 for overseas citizens and voters with disabilities[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-utah-mobile-voting-case-study-accessibility-and-expanding-voting-options#:~:text=to%20offer%20mobile%20voting,The%20voting)[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-utah-mobile-voting-case-study-accessibility-and-expanding-voting-options#:~:text=With%20this%20success%2C%20Utah%20County,in%20the%20eventual%20goal%20of). In total, Voatz reported that as of late 2020, it had facilitated about 15 small-scale election pilots across various jurisdictions in the U.S. These were all relatively limited in scope (often a few hundred voters at most) – a deliberate strategy to test the waters. Internationally, Voatz has been more limited; the company’s focus has been U.S. elections, working within the framework of state pilots. One high-profile deployment was the _2019 Utah Republican Party Convention_, where delegates (unable to meet in person due to COVID-19) voted for their party nominees via the Voatz app. This was a private political event, but it demonstrated the appeal of mobile voting in the pandemic context.

**Partnerships and Collaborations:** Voatz’s efforts have been supported by philanthropic and academic partners. _Tusk Philanthropies_, a nonprofit advocating for mobile voting, funded many of the pilots (including West Virginia and Utah) and worked with local officials to implement the technology[govtech.com](https://www.govtech.com/biz/Detailed-Audit-of-Voatz-Voting-App-Confirms-Security-Flaws.html#:~:text=Voatz%20itself%2C%20together%20with%20mobile,low%2C%20undetermined%20and%20informational%20severity). The _National Cybersecurity Center (NCC)_, a Colorado-based nonprofit, has been another key partner – NCC observers have audited Voatz elections in multiple states, lending independent oversight[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-utah-mobile-voting-case-study-accessibility-and-expanding-voting-options#:~:text=match%20at%20L154%20With%20this,in%20the%20eventual%20goal%20of)[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-utah-mobile-voting-case-study-accessibility-and-expanding-voting-options#:~:text=With%20this%20success%2C%20Utah%20County,in%20the%20eventual%20goal%20of). On the corporate side, Voatz attracted investment from **Overstock.com’s** blockchain venture arm (Medici Ventures) and TechStars, indicating investor interest in this niche. Going forward, Voatz is positioning itself to serve election agencies as a **turnkey mobile voting solution** for absentee voters. Its market footprint is still small (pilots in a handful of U.S. states), but it has arguably the most field experience in mobile voting so far. The company’s reputation has been a mix of innovation and caution – election officials are intrigued by the success stories (e.g., disabled voters in West Virginia praising the ease of voting by phone, and measurable turnout improvements[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=A%20volunteer%20in%20a%20remote,30%20countries%20around%20the%20world)), but also wary due to the security concerns raised by experts. Voatz’s journey highlights the tension between adopting new tech and satisfying the scrutiny that any voting system demands.

### 3.2 Scytl

Scytl is a Spanish company and a veteran in electronic voting technology. Founded in 2001 in Barcelona as a spin-off from academic research, Scytl (pronounced “sigh-tul”) has developed a suite of election solutions, including online voting platforms, electronic poll books, and results management systems. It became one of the **largest providers of internet voting systems globally**, involved in projects across Europe, North America, and Asia. Scytl’s technology often operates behind the scenes for governments – for example, providing a secure portal for overseas voters or an online ballot delivery system.

**Technology:** Scytl’s flagship online voting system (often branded as _Pnyx_) employs **end-to-end cryptographic protocols** to protect votes. The company has patented techniques for mixing and shuffling encrypted votes to break any link between voter identity and the ballot, aiming to ensure anonymity. They advertise features like voter-verifiable casting codes, digital signatures on ballots, and strong encryption from the voter’s device through to the digital ballot box. In Switzerland, Scytl partnered with Swiss Post to implement a highly secure e-voting system: it claimed to use **end-to-end encryption that only the official electoral board could decrypt**, with sophisticated zero-knowledge proofs to enable verification of the tally[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=and%20the%20Barcelona,and%20would%20be%20responsible%20for). However, implementing such complex cryptography correctly is challenging. In 2019, Swiss authorities opened Scytl’s system to a public penetration test – and cryptography experts discovered serious problems. They found that due to a flaw in the mix-net proof, an attacker with insider access could alter votes undetectably, undermining the claim of end-to-end verifiability[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=Cryptography%20experts%20who%20spent%20just,the%20system%20are%20done%20properly)[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=Even%20if%20the%20system%20is,the%20system%20and%20alter%20votes). Likewise, an earlier Scytl-based system in New South Wales (Australia’s largest state) suffered a vulnerability: researchers in 2015 showed they could bypass encryption and reveal votes because the system did not properly implement verification safeguards[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=match%20at%20L174%20In%202015%2C,Another%20group%20of%20researchers). Scytl acknowledged and fixed these issues, but these incidents highlight that even with strong crypto on paper, _practical security depends on flawless implementation_. Scytl’s technology stack typically includes secure voter authentication (often via personal codes and passwords issued to each voter), an encrypted voting session (through a web or mobile interface), and a back-end election server that tallies votes after mixing/decrypting them. They also focus on auditability – providing hashed logs and audit trails – though critics have sometimes noted a lack of transparency (in one case, Scytl’s documentation for Switzerland had confidentiality clauses limiting what could be shared publicly[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=match%20at%20L232%20questions%20about,In%20the)[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=period,the%20public%20or%20otherwise%20distributed)). In recent years, Scytl has worked on improving transparency, especially after the Swiss experience, and has even open-sourced parts of its code in certain jurisdictions. Overall, Scytl’s tech is viewed as sophisticated but was proprietary; this led some governments (like Switzerland) to demand more openness before proceeding further.

**Market Footprint:** Scytl has had an extensive global footprint. By the late 2010s, the company claimed to have conducted over 100 online voting projects in more than **20 countries**. A 2019 investigative report noted that _Scytl isn’t a small player in elections – it has provided online voting solutions for national or regional elections in 42 countries_[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=questions%20about%20other%20Scytl%20systems,In%20the). These include European countries such as France (which used Scytl’s system for overseas voters in legislative elections), Switzerland (multiple canton trials from 2003–2019), Austria (experiments in student union elections), Norway (pilots in 2011 and 2013 municipal elections), and Australia (the iVote system in NSW). In Canada, Scytl’s software has powered municipal elections – for instance, the city of Markham’s early adoption of internet voting and dozens of Ontario municipalities that introduced online ballots had Scytl’s involvement at some point. In the United States, Scytl made inroads by providing **electronic ballot delivery** platforms for military voters: at one time, **1,300+ U.S. counties** were using a Scytl system to deliver blank ballots to overseas voters (who would then print and return them)[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=internet%20and%20other%20voting%20solutions,In%20the). Notably, Scytl was not generally tabulating votes over the internet in the U.S.; it was more about ballot distribution and other election management products. The company also acquired SOE Software, an American firm, and through that provided online election night reporting for many U.S. jurisdictions. Scytl’s growth hit a bump around 2020 – the company filed for bankruptcy amid financial difficulties, and it was acquired by an investor group (its new parent company is **Service Point Solutions/Paragon Group** as of late 2020)[marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/quote/stock/INNOVATIVE-SOLUTIONS-ECOS-32676224/news/Service-Point-Solutions-S-A-acquired-Scytl-Secure-Electronic-Voting-S-A-33660591/#:~:text=Share). This restructuring aimed to keep Scytl’s operations going. Indeed, Scytl solutions continue to be used; for example, India’s online voting trials for certain local elections in 2022 used a platform that drew on Scytl technology. In summary, Scytl has been a **market leader in online voting**, especially for government-run pilots and binding elections in Europe. Its systems have recorded **millions of votes** over two decades. However, some high-profile failures (like the Swiss Post system being withdrawn after the pen test findings) have also made it a case study in the challenges of internet voting security.

**Reputation and Partnerships:** Scytl often worked hand-in-hand with government election commissions and major IT integrators. For the Swiss project, Swiss Post was the face, with Scytl as the technology provider – a partnership that became strained after the vulnerability disclosures[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=Switzerland%20made%20headlines%20this%20month,of%20the%20system%20to%20attack)[vice.com](https://www.vice.com/en/article/experts-find-serious-problems-with-switzerlands-online-voting-system-before-public-penetration-test-even-begins/#:~:text=the%20negative%20comments%2C%20discuss%20them,%E2%80%9D). In Australia, Scytl collaborated with local election officials to deploy iVote, and after initial hiccups, that system served over 280,000 voters in the 2015 NSW election (though it later faced other issues unrelated to security). Scytl also partnered with **Microsoft** in providing election modernization tools (interestingly, Microsoft’s ElectionGuard can complement systems like Scytl’s by adding audit layers). In the realm of security, Scytl engaged independent experts on occasion and touted endorsements by institutions (e.g., the European Commission awarded grants supporting Scytl’s R&D). Despite that, within the election security community, Scytl has sometimes been viewed with skepticism due to its closed-source approach and the complexity of its cryptographic protocols. The 2020 U.S. election brought Scytl unwelcome notoriety when conspiracy theories falsely claimed Scytl servers “flipped votes” – purely a baseless rumor, but it shows how a lack of public understanding about such companies can fuel mistrust. Scytl publicly refuted those claims, and officials confirmed there was no such involvement. Going forward, Scytl (now under new ownership) is focusing on its core software and likely will continue as a prominent vendor in online voting for **national elections, party elections, and municipal votes**. The company’s longevity and wide adoption give it a deep well of experience, making it a key reference point in any discussion of mobile or online voting.

### 3.3 ElectionGuard

ElectionGuard is not a company but an **open-source security toolkit** for voting systems, initiated by Microsoft’s **Defending Democracy Program**. Launched in 2019, ElectionGuard aims to make elections _end-to-end verifiable_ using advanced cryptography, and it is provided freely for incorporation into voting software or hardware. While ElectionGuard is often associated with ballot-scanning machines (optical scanners) and voting machines, its principles apply equally to online or mobile voting. It represents a collaborative, transparent approach to election security rather than a commercial product.

**Technology:** At its core, ElectionGuard uses **homomorphic encryption and zero-knowledge proofs** to ensure that votes are properly counted without revealing any voter’s selections. When integrated into a voting system, ElectionGuard will encrypt each vote with a public key as it’s cast. It then produces a **tracking code** (a checksum or hash) that is given to the voter as a receipt. The encryption is special – it allows mathematical addition on the ciphertexts. So all encrypted votes can be combined (added) to get an encrypted tally, which can be later decrypted _only_ to reveal the aggregate totals, not individual votes. This addresses the confidentiality aspect: ballots remain secret. Meanwhile, the **tracking code** lets a voter go online after the election and input their code to verify that their vote is indeed among those counted and that it wasn’t changed[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=What%20does%20ElectionGuard%20do%3F)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=Election%20monitors%20carry%20out%20spot,end%20verifiability). The system will show something like “Your vote was counted” (but not how the vote was, preserving secrecy). Additionally, ElectionGuard publishes the **encrypted votes and all the cryptographic proofs** on a public bulletin board. Outside observers – from political parties, media, to nerdy citizens – can use the open-source ElectionGuard verifier to check that the published tally is mathematically consistent with the published encrypted votes and proofs. In effect, anyone can run their own audit of the outcome without needing to trust the election authority’s software. Crucially, **if any vote were altered or dropped**, the public audit would detect a mismatch and reveal that the results are not valid[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=ElectionGuard%20is%20a%20way%20of,an%20accurate%20and%20fair%20result)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/03/27/what-is-electionguard/#:~:text=Because%20attacks%20cannot%20always%20be,That%20requires%20stringent%20auditing). ElectionGuard also employs **secure multiparty techniques**: the decryption key for the final tally can be split among multiple trustees (e.g., representatives from different parties), so no single person can decrypt votes alone. This distributed trust model and open auditing make ElectionGuard a powerful addition to voting systems. It’s important to note that ElectionGuard _by itself is not a voting system_ – it doesn’t handle things like voter login or UI. For mobile voting, a vendor could integrate ElectionGuard’s encryption library into their app, thereby gaining these verification features. The toolkit is still evolving (as of 2024, a reference implementation in Python and C was available on GitHub), but it has been praised by security experts as a big step toward **software-independent, verifiable elections**.

**Deployments and Adoption:** Despite being new, ElectionGuard has already seen use in several pilot elections. According to Microsoft, ElectionGuard has been _integrated into a variety of systems and used in actual public elections in the U.S._ – including pilots in **Wisconsin, California, Idaho, Utah, and Maryland** – as well as in a trial for a **U.S. Congress caucus election**, and even a local election in France[eprint.iacr.org](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/955.pdf#:~:text=candidates%2C%20media%2C%20and%20even%20voters,the%20separation%20of%20the%20cryptographic). One of the first pilots was in Fulton, Wisconsin in 2019: voters filled out paper ballots as usual, but an ElectionGuard-enabled machine scanned and encrypted those ballots, allowing voters to get a tracking code and later verify their vote was counted correctly. The official outcome was still determined by paper ballots, but the pilot proved the technology works alongside traditional systems. Another notable use was in an election in **King County, Washington** (which was a virtual election for a board of advisors) – this was a fully online election using VotingWorks (a nonprofit voting tech company) and ElectionGuard to encrypt votes; participants could verify their votes online through the ElectionGuard portal. Additionally, outside the U.S., a suburb of Paris, France used ElectionGuard for a municipal election pilot, and an international organization in Switzerland/Denmark employed it for an internal election[eprint.iacr.org](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/955.pdf#:~:text=of%20systems%20and%20used%20in,the%20separation%20of%20the%20cryptographic). These real-world tests, though small in scale, demonstrate ElectionGuard’s versatility across different environments. It’s gaining interest from various voting system vendors: **Smartmatic**, a major election technology company, announced plans to incorporate ElectionGuard into its systems, and **Clear Ballot** (a U.S. voting machine vendor) has also been exploring it. Because it’s open-source, even smaller startups or academic projects can adopt ElectionGuard without licensing costs.

**Community and Impact:** ElectionGuard represents a shift toward _open, verifiable elections_. Its development team includes renowned cryptographers (like Josh Benaloh at Microsoft Research) and it underwent academic peer review (a 2024 technical paper details its design and real-world learnings[eprint.iacr.org](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/955.pdf#:~:text=ElectionGuard%20is%20a%20flexible%20set,been%20used%20for%20civic%20voting)[eprint.iacr.org](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/955.pdf#:~:text=design%2C%20not%20novel%2C%20some%20significant,while%20he%20was%20at%20Rice)). The initiative has partnerships with Galois (an Oregon-based security firm that helped build it) and support from the U.S. Department of Defense DARPA (which co-funded some development under an effort to secure voting). By providing the toolkit free, Microsoft hopes to raise the security baseline of voting systems worldwide – whether paper-based, machine-based, or mobile. ElectionGuard doesn’t directly solve all of mobile voting’s challenges (for example, it doesn’t stop a hacker from attacking a voter’s device), but it can make attacks far more detectable and thus less likely to succeed unnoticed. A potential future scenario is a mobile voting app that uses ElectionGuard: voters would cast on their phone, get a tracking code, and after the election could verify their vote in the public tally – combining convenience with high assurance. The concept of **“software independence”**, recommended by the U.S. National Academies, is embodied in tools like ElectionGuard (meaning the election outcome can be independently checked without relying on trusting the software). In sum, ElectionGuard is a leading _technological framework_ that many in the election community see as key to **future secure voting**. Its presence on the list of key “players” (often cited alongside companies) is because it’s driving innovation and being adopted by multiple platforms, rather than competing as a product.

## 4\. Adoption and Regulatory Landscape

The rollout of secure mobile voting technologies varies widely around the world. Some jurisdictions have eagerly piloted these systems, aiming to boost turnout or serve voters who face barriers with traditional voting, while others remain cautious or have legal prohibitions due to security concerns. This section examines **global adoption trends**, highlighting where mobile/online voting has been tried, and reviews the **regulatory and public trust factors** influencing its spread.

-   **Global Adoption Trends:** A few pioneering countries have implemented internet voting (which often includes the option to vote via personal devices) on a significant scale. The most cited example is **Estonia**, which has offered nationwide internet voting since 2005. Estonian citizens can vote online in national elections using a government-issued digital ID; they often do so from their home computers or smartphones. Over the years usage has steadily grown – in the **March 2023 parliamentary elections, 51% of all votes were cast online**, marking the first time online votes accounted for over half of votes countrywide[e-estonia.com](https://e-estonia.com/how-did-estonia-carry-out-the-worlds-first-mostly-online-national-elections/#:~:text=How%20did%20Estonia%20carry%20out,voting%20since%202005). This demonstrates that, given a long track record and trust, remote e-voting can achieve high uptake. Estonia’s system uses strong digital signatures and a form of verifiable encryption (and interestingly, even they are updating their system to incorporate more advanced cryptography akin to ElectionGuard’s approach). Outside of Estonia, **small nations and local governments** have been the next most avid adopters. In **Switzerland**, several cantons experimented with online voting for expatriates and some local referendums for years. The Swiss federal government set a goal to make e-voting a “third voting channel” alongside polling stations and mail. However, after security researchers exposed flaws in the Swiss Post/Scytl system in 2019, Switzerland paused and is now re-evaluating with a new, more open-source system. A few cantons are expected to reintroduce e-voting in a limited form by 2024, but with heavy scrutiny. **Canada** has seen a lot of online voting at the municipal level. Notably, in the province of Ontario, many city elections use online/phone voting: _as of the 2018 municipal elections, about 45% of Ontario municipalities (accounting for 29% of voters in the province) offered an online voting option_[docs.electionsquebec.qc.ca](https://docs.electionsquebec.qc.ca/ORG/5ee12ee324ff3/Essex_Akinyokun_Cardillo_02-11-2019_article_scient.pdf#:~:text=,offered%20online%20voting). This translates to hundreds of thousands of Canadians voting via internet in local elections (estimated around 1 million online municipal votes in Ontario 2018) – generally without major incident, though there was a network slowdown in 2018 that caused some cities to extend voting hours. In **Australia**, the state of New South Wales allowed internet voting (iVote) for distant and disabled voters in state elections from 2011 through 2019, at its peak serving over 200,000 voters, until it was suspended due to a combination of security and reliability concerns. **Brazil** and **India**, which use electronic voting machines nationwide, have not moved to internet voting for public political elections (security experts in those countries have advised against it for now), though India’s Election Commission has contemplated a system for migrant voters. In **Latin America**, some countries have used online voting for expatriates (e.g., Mexico had a system for overseas voters in 2021). **Partial adoption** is common: many countries allow overseas citizens or military personnel to vote electronically (often via web portals or email) as an exception, even if regular voters cannot. The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 created pressure to explore remote voting, but most large democracies resisted deploying mobile voting widely on short notice, opting instead for expanded postal voting. Nevertheless, a few U.S. states did temporarily broaden electronic ballot return for certain voters during the pandemic (for example, emails or online portal returns for voters quarantining, in states like New Jersey and West Virginia). **Private sector and organizations** have also embraced mobile voting in non-government elections: from corporate shareholder meetings to union votes and university student government elections, various online voting platforms (ElectionBuddy, Simply Voting, etc.) are routinely used, showing the demand for convenient voting in those contexts. These are less constrained by public law and often see smooth usage, albeit with lower security requirements than public-government elections.
-   **United States Landscape:** The U.S. has seen only **limited adoption** of mobile voting, primarily in pilot programs. No U.S. state currently offers mobile or online voting to all citizens in standard elections. However, as discussed, **West Virginia**, **Utah**, **Colorado (Denver)**, **Oregon** and a few others have run pilots targeting _military and overseas voters_ or _voters with disabilities_. About 30 states do allow some form of **electronic return of ballots** for overseas or military voters – but typically this is via fax or email attachment, which are considered quite insecure. Those methods persist as a last resort for voters who can’t feasibly return a paper ballot in time. The pilots with purpose-built mobile apps (like Voatz or Democracy Live’s OmniBallot) were meant to be more secure than email. After 2020, there has been a mix of interest and concern. On one hand, states like **West Virginia** passed legislation to keep exploring mobile voting for those with disabilities[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=West%20Virginia%20continues%20to%20explore,15%20217%20citizens), citing the successful use by disabled voters in 2020. On the other hand, states like **Colorado** (which had allowed a small Denver pilot) have since banned internet ballot returns outside of narrow exceptions, aligning with experts’ warnings. The U.S. Congress has not explicitly legislated on mobile voting, but federal bodies like the **Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)** and the **Election Assistance Commission (EAC)** have issued guidance. In 2020, CISA, EAC, the FBI, and NIST jointly assessed that **electronic ballot return is high-risk and should be limited to voters who have no other alternative**[cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-02/Final_%20Risk_Management_for_Electronic-Ballot_05082020_508c.pdf#:~:text=The%20Cybersecurity%20and%20Infrastructure%20Security,Recognizing%20that%20some%20election%20officials). They “recommend paper ballot return” for the foreseeable future and note that even the best controls cannot fully eliminate the risks of large-scale internet voting[cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-02/Final_%20Risk_Management_for_Electronic-Ballot_05082020_508c.pdf#:~:text=Assistance%20Commission%20,state%20law%20to%20employ%20this)[cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-02/Final_%20Risk_Management_for_Electronic-Ballot_05082020_508c.pdf#:~:text=voter%E2%80%99s%20ballot%20Electronic%20ballot%20return,and%2C%20can%20occur%20at%20scale). Similarly, an authoritative 2018 report by the National Academy of Sciences stated “we do not, at present, have the technology to offer a secure Internet voting option” – though it allowed that future advancements could change that. This essentially sets a cautious tone that influences regulators.
-   **Regulatory and Legal Barriers:** Many jurisdictions have legal provisions that impede the adoption of mobile voting. **Election law** often requires a secret ballot and a voter-verified permanent record. Ensuring a “secret ballot” in a remote setting is tricky – laws may prohibit anyone other than the voter from seeing their choices, yet if someone votes on a phone at home, there’s no guarantee against coercion or family pressure. Some states interpret that risk as a reason to forbid remote voting for general populations. Additionally, certification standards (in the U.S., the federal Voluntary Voting System Guidelines) currently do not cover internet voting systems, which means there is no clear certification path – states would be on their own to vet a system. In Europe, the Council of Europe issued guidelines for e-voting (requiring that systems be as secure and transparent as traditional methods). Countries like **Norway** and **France** rolled back internet voting for expatriates after trial runs, due to security and political concerns. France used internet voting for overseas citizens in legislative elections in 2012, but canceled it for 2017 after intelligence warned of cyber threats; they planned to reintroduce a more secure system in 2021 for consular elections. This back-and-forth shows that legal approval often hinges on the current cyber threat environment. **Public Trust and Perception:** Regulatory decisions are also driven by public and expert perception. In many places, there is significant **public skepticism** about the safety of internet voting – often informed by computer scientists’ near-universal warnings about current systems’ vulnerabilities[aaas.org](https://www.aaas.org/epi-center/internet-online-voting#:~:text=Internet%20or%20Online%20Voting%20Remains,is%20no%20technical%20evidence). High-profile cybersecurity organizations and associations (like AAAS and Verified Voting in the U.S.) have actively advised governments that mobile or online voting should not be deployed for public elections yet, given the risks. This creates political reluctance: lawmakers don’t want to be responsible for an election disaster. On the other hand, segments of the public, especially younger or overseas voters, express frustration that so much of life can be done securely online _except voting_. This has led to advocacy groups pushing for change and carefully controlled pilots to demonstrate feasibility. **Legal liability** is another concern – if a mobile voting system were compromised, it could lead to election invalidation and lawsuits. Some election officials feel that until a system is federally certified or endorsed by a broad consensus of experts, adopting it is not worth the risk. Hence, the regulatory landscape is one of cautious experimentation: small pilots are often allowed under special administrative rules (or emergency pandemic rules), but broader implementation runs into legal roadblocks. Over time, if pilots continue to show positive results and security technology improves, laws may be updated. For example, a proposed **Utah state bill** in 2020 sought to expand mobile voting pilots to any municipality that wants to try, giving local officials authority to decide how and for whom (this came after Utah County’s success and was a sign of growing legislative support)[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-utah-mobile-voting-case-study-accessibility-and-expanding-voting-options#:~:text=match%20at%20L171%20Mike%20Winder,debate%20in%20the%20state%20Senate).
-   **Standards and Certification Efforts:** Recognizing the gap in standards, some organizations are working on frameworks for internet voting. The **Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)** has a project for standardizing electronic voting machine security, possibly extendable to online voting. Also, **NIST** has been researching remote voting risks and guidelines (NISTIR 8310 in 2022 outlined considerations for internet voting, essentially echoing that it should be limited until certain security milestones are met). Government agencies are also insisting on certain features if mobile voting is used: end-to-end verifiability, voter privacy protections, and auditable results are becoming baseline expectations from a regulatory standpoint. **Data protection laws** (like GDPR) impose requirements on how voter data (personal info, biometrics) is handled in these systems, which companies must comply with – including obtaining consent, allowing voters to request deletion of personal data after the election, etc. This adds another layer of compliance that influences system design (for instance, Voatz deleting personal identity data after verification to minimize privacy risk[voatz.com](https://voatz.com/type/5-how-voatz-works/#:~:text=Protecting%20all%20voters%E2%80%99%20personal%20information,authenticate%20the%20voter%20going%20forward)).

In summary, adoption of secure mobile voting is proceeding **gradually and carefully**. Pockets of real-world use (military/expat voters, local elections) show that the technology can work and even improve participation. However, regulatory and public confidence hurdles mean that for most countries, **mobile voting in high-stakes national elections is still on the horizon**. Ongoing pilots and evolving laws – like those in West Virginia, Utah, and some European countries – will likely pave the way, if they continue to demonstrate security and reliability.

## 5\. Future Prospects and Opportunities

Looking ahead, the intersection of emerging technology and electoral policy will shape how (and if) mobile voting becomes mainstream. The next decade could bring significant advancements that make mobile voting more secure and widely accepted, but there are also challenges on the horizon. Here we outline the future prospects, including technological developments, policy evolution, and opportunities for innovation and market leadership:

-   **Advancements in Security Technology:** The continual progress in fields like cryptography, cybersecurity, and mobile hardware will directly benefit mobile voting security. We can expect **stronger encryption algorithms** (especially with an eye on quantum-resistant encryption to future-proof the confidentiality of ballots). Techniques such as **zero-knowledge proofs** will be further refined to allow verification of election integrity without revealing any private information – this could enable, for example, voters to get an ironclad proof that their vote was counted in the tally, all while preserving anonymity. **Homomorphic encryption** will likely become more efficient and standardized, making it feasible to tally large elections with encrypted votes quickly. Secure multi-party frameworks might get baked into national election infrastructures, meaning multiple institutions (e.g., election commission, courts, parties) jointly hold the keys to the kingdom, distributing trust. Additionally, the ubiquity of **trusted hardware** in smartphones (secure enclaves, TPMs, etc.) is an opportunity: future mobile voting apps could run critical cryptographic operations in isolated secure environments on the phone, immune to malware on the main OS. There’s research into using the same chips that store your FaceID or fingerprint data to also store voting keys, ensuring that even if the phone is compromised, the vote remains secure. Another area of growth is **biometric technology** – it will become more sophisticated (e.g., liveness detection to prevent deepfake-style spoofing of face or voice). As national digital ID programs expand (for instance, mobile driver's licenses or government ID apps), they could be integrated into voter authentication, streamlining the onboarding of voters in a secure way. We may see a scenario where a country’s digital ID app has a “voting” feature enabled during election season, combining secure ID verification with the act of casting a ballot, thus leveraging an already trusted platform.
-   **Policy and Regulatory Evolution:** For mobile voting to gain broad acceptance, policy has to catch up with technology. In the coming years, we will likely see more jurisdictions drafting **regulations specifically for electronic voting**. These may include stringent certification requirements – for example, requiring any mobile voting system to undergo white-box penetration testing, open-source code review, and public pilots before it can be used legally in binding elections. As technology proves itself in limited deployments, lawmakers could become more comfortable. If, for instance, a state runs mobile voting for overseas voters for several election cycles with no incidents and improved participation, that state might legislate to expand it to other absentee voters (like those in remote rural areas, or voters with certain hardships). **Standards bodies** might also step in: a framework akin to the VVSG could emerge for internet voting. Internationally, countries might share best practices – we can imagine an exchange between Estonia’s experience and, say, states in the U.S., resulting in published guidelines on how to implement verifiable mobile voting securely. Another policy aspect is addressing the **coercion concern**: laws might be passed that allow a voter who casts a vote online to cancel or change their vote by voting in person later (Estonia already does this – online votes can be overridden by an in-person vote, which helps mitigate family coercion or vote-buying, since the bad actor can never be sure the voter didn’t later cancel the online vote). Such legal safeguards, combined with tech, can alleviate some social risks of remote voting. Governments may also invest in **voter education campaigns** about mobile voting, emphasizing security features and proper use, to build public trust. Crucially, public trust can be cemented if high-profile pilot programs go well; positive narratives (e.g., military voters successfully voting from war zones via secure apps) will help counteract the fear of the unknown. On the flip side, a single major failure or breach could set back policy acceptance by years, so early implementations will likely remain conservative.
-   **Wider Adoption and Market Growth:** Assuming steady technological improvement and cautious expansion, we could see mobile voting options become relatively common for certain segments by the late 2020s. **Overseas citizens and military personnel** are likely to be the first beneficiaries on a broader scale (many countries are motivated to solve the low turnout in this group). **Voters with disabilities** are another group that will drive adoption – accessibility advocates in the U.S. have already filed lawsuits in some states to allow electronic ballot return for those who cannot mark a paper ballot privately. As these legal pressures mount, states may opt for secure mobile solutions rather than the very insecure email/fax methods currently in use. **Local elections and referendums** might serve as testbeds as well: for instance, a city might allow mobile voting in a low-turnout municipal election or a party primary to see how it goes. Internationally, countries with a tech-forward outlook (perhaps some in Europe or Asia with strong digital infrastructure) may initiate new trials. We might also see **regional leadership** – just as Estonia became a model in Europe, perhaps a U.S. state like Utah could become a model in America by gradually scaling up their mobile voting and sharing results. The **market for online voting software is projected to grow** significantly. Estimates suggest the global online election voting market size could reach about **$737 million by 2030 (up from ~$293 million in 2022)**, nearly 10% compound annual growth[globenewswire.com](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2023/05/10/2665334/0/en/Online-Election-Voting-Software-Market-Size-Expected-to-Reach-USD-737-2-Million-by-2030-With-9-9-CAGR-Exclusive-Report-by-Zion-Market-Research-Global-Online-Election-Voting-Softwar.html#:~:text=,Voatz%2C%20Votem%2C%20VotingWorks%2C%20and%20others)[globenewswire.com](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2023/05/10/2665334/0/en/Online-Election-Voting-Software-Market-Size-Expected-to-Reach-USD-737-2-Million-by-2030-With-9-9-CAGR-Exclusive-Report-by-Zion-Market-Research-Global-Online-Election-Voting-Softwar.html#:~:text=%E2%80%9CAccording%20to%20the%20latest%20research,%E2%80%9D). This indicates that many players (from startups to established election companies) are investing in this area, anticipating future demand.
-   **Opportunities for Innovation and Leadership:** The coming years present opportunities for both technology companies and governments to lead in this space. On the tech side, companies that can **demonstrate rock-solid security and transparency** will stand out. For example, a vendor that offers a fully open-source mobile voting platform with end-to-end verifiability and has undergone comprehensive third-party security audits could position itself as a trustworthy provider when governments look for solutions. There is an opportunity for **new entrants** as well – perhaps leveraging blockchain in novel ways or integrating AI for smart fraud detection (though AI must be used carefully to avoid black-box issues). Even big tech firms could enter the fray: one could imagine, say, a secure voting module added to widely used authentication apps or cloud platforms, offered as a public service. The **open-source community** might also deliver reference designs that smaller jurisdictions can adopt without huge cost. For governments and election officials, there is an opportunity to **lead through experimentation** and setting standards. For instance, states that create a clear legal pathway for pilots and form advisory boards of security experts to oversee them will be seen as proactive. Those that collaborate internationally (sharing audit data, inviting global experts to evaluate their systems) will help establish best practices. Over time, such leadership can influence national policy – e.g., if a handful of states successfully use mobile voting for all absentee voters by 2028 with robust audits, the pressure will mount on others to consider it, especially if it demonstrably improves turnout or convenience.
-   **Addressing Future Threats:** It’s also important to consider that as security tech improves, **threats will evolve**. Attackers might employ more sophisticated methods, like AI-driven phishing at scale, deepfake audio/video to fool biometric checks, or even quantum computing (down the line) to attempt decryption. The election community will need to stay a step ahead. This means ongoing security research and possibly building **resilience into systems** (for example, designing mobile voting to always have a paper backup or fallback option, so even in worst-case scenarios the election can continue). The silver lining is that many of the emerging technologies are _dual-use_ – the same AI that can create fake videos can also be used to detect them; the same quantum computing that threatens encryption also inspires quantum-safe algorithms. Election defense will remain a cat-and-mouse game, but greater collaboration between governments (treating election infrastructure as critical national security infrastructure) will help. We might see, for example, **continuous penetration testing “bug bounty” programs** for any mobile voting system in use – inviting global white-hat hackers year-round, rather than just before an election.

In conclusion, the path to secure mobile voting becoming a regular part of democracy is cautious but hopeful. Technological innovations are steadily knocking down the barriers – making it possible to verify election outcomes and protect votes in ways that were theoretical a decade ago. The strategic focus in the near future will be on **demonstrating reliability at small scales, earning trust through transparency, and incrementally expanding scope**. If stakeholders prioritize security, testing, and auditability at every step, mobile voting could transform from a niche pilot into a **trusted component of electoral systems**, particularly for those who otherwise struggle to vote. The ultimate opportunity is to make voting more accessible and convenient _without_ sacrificing integrity – achieving that will be a significant democratic accomplishment.

**Actionable Insights:** For election leaders contemplating mobile voting, a few clear insights emerge from this analysis: (1) **Start small and audit everything** – begin with controlled pilots (for overseas or disabled voters) and subject the process to rigorous independent security audits and voter-verified audits[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/updates/the-west-virginia-mobile-voting-case-study-providing-a-convenient-and-secure-voting-option-for-uniformed-service-members#:~:text=person%20and%20independently%20by%20mail,any%20internal%20or%20external%20tampering). This builds confidence and exposes issues early. (2) **Leverage the latest tech but don’t black-box it** – use innovations like blockchain and E2E encryption to improve security, but make the system transparent (open source code, publish cryptographic proofs) so experts and the public can verify claims[mobilevoting.org](https://www.mobilevoting.org/how-it-works#:~:text=). (3) **Focus on user-centric design** – invest in the voter experience and support, ensuring accessibility features and contingency options; security is only effective if voters can and will use the system properly. (4) **Engage lawmakers and the public** – work with legislators to update laws in tandem with pilot results, and educate voters on how the technology protects their vote, to build trust and demand. By following these steps and remaining vigilant about evolving threats, jurisdictions can position themselves at the forefront of secure mobile voting, ultimately reaping the benefits of higher participation and a more inclusive democracy while upholding election integrity.

Blockchain technology, biometric authentication, end-to-end encryption, and secure multi-party computation (MPC) are pivotal in enhancing mobile voting systems.
